description: Hannah and Marco's team and also ines aswell
summary: We developed an offline voice based health companion that will run entirely on a spacecraft's own computer. Bento reads each crew member's vital signs as well as environmental data and compares to a normal baseline. It speaks out when something changes, logs symptoms in the crew's own words, runs morning check ins and provides instructions through protocol cards based off NASA and first aid sources. A locally run language model converses with the crew however every number, alert and emergency decision stems purely from plain, tested code.
details:
What it does:

Bento answers health questions from real data, if you ask it how you are doing it compares your vital signs to your normal base levels. If an emergency is detected, I.E a solar storm or high CO2 levels, code will sound an emergency alarm, then read protocols to crew members based off NASA data. Bento will then provide answers to any follow up questions.

Emergency scenarios can be simulated from the dashboard and Bento will react in real time without a script. In our demo it links a crew member's headache to rising CO2, using NASA's ISS finding.

Bento logs any reported symptoms and asks for a 0-10 severity scale.

In an emergency, hard code bypasses the AI and raises the alarm with minimal delay.

Bento runs morning check ins for fatigue, mood, stress and any other reported symptoms.

Everything is shown on a mission control dashboard with live vital sign charts, CO2 chart including NASA's limit and flashing alerts along with a transcript of everything that has been said.

How it works:

Inputted speech will be transcribed by faster-whisper on the CPU, code will check it for emergency phrases then pass it on to Qwen3.5-9B which runs locally on the GPU. The LLM reads health data using 8 tool calls into a deterministic monitoring engine which can compute baselines, changes, trends and alert levels. Before anything is outputted hard code will filter the reply. Every number must originate from the data or a crewmate's words. Anything that attempts to diagnose or invent figures is shut down. Replies are outputted with Kokoro text to speech running on the CPU. The voice, engine and dashboard all share an SQLite database. Guidance stems from protocol cards, each listing it's source, NASA or otherwise.

We tested it with 23 integration checks (automated) and 12 conversation scenarios. These include safety checks such as refusing to generate data that doesn't exist and declining to tell someone that they are okay when data shows otherwise.

Everything was able to run smoothly on a consumer desktop PC (Ryzen 7 3700X, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2070 8 GB), with about 2 to 3.5 seconds of model time per reply.

Benefits:

Alerts crew immediately of danger, Can operate with no link to earth, no health data ever leaves the spacecraft, hands free voice operation, individually assesses each crew members vitals, alert crew immediately of danger, every number comes from data and it honestly says when it doesn't know instead of hallucinating figures.

TOOLS

Python 3.11 on Ubuntu; llama.cpp with Qwen3.5-9B; faster-whisper (Whisper small.en); Kokoro-82M text-to-speech; Streamlit, Altair and pandas; SQLite. Hardware: one desktop PC with an RTX 2070.

All simulated data was generated by our own code. No copyrighted text, image or audio were used.
